newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil pols spare no expense in battle for votes.
newsitem.headline: Brazil pols spare no expense in battle for votes.

text.p: Brazilians go to the polls Thursday in the first round of nationwide municipal elections after an extravagant U.S.-style campaign in which candidates spared no expense in the battle for votes.

The elections, which will decide who runs city hall in over 5,000 municipalities across the country, has generated a multi-million dollar industry employing hundreds of marketing advisers and thousands of logistical staff.

Analysts estimate that in a rich constituency like the city of Sao Paulo, where 6.7 million people will vote this week, the two leading candidates will have easily spent over $50 million each at the end of the five month campaign.
Even in a medium-sized state capital like Boa Vista, in Brazil's Amazon state of Roraima, a candidate for mayor must spend $2 million to $3 million to finance his campaign.

"This has been, without a doubt, the most expensive and sophisticated campaign Brazil has ever seen," said Gaudencio Torquato, a campaign marketing specialist and professor at Sao Paulo University (USP).

With one Latin America's youngest electorates, which learned to vote after the military surrendered power to the civilians in the mid 1980's, Brazilian campaigns are short on ideology and long on marketing.
This has generated a small but powerful group of image specialists who have virtually taken over all aspects of a candidate's campaign.

Newspapers reported Celso Pitta, the front-runner in the Sao Paulo mayor's race, will reward Dudu Mendonca, the strategist behind his glossy television campaign, with between $3 million to $4 million if he wins the election.

Pitta, a political neophite who has never run for public office, spent over 15 million in TV advertisments in which he used sophisticated computer graphics to show voters how he planned to transform Sao Paulo's public transport system.

Pitta's campaign staff say it is money well spent. The winner of the Sao Paulo mayoral election will manage an annual budget of over $6 billion. If lucky, he might even win a shot at the governor's or even the president's office in a few years time.
Analysts said funding for these campaigns comes mostly from major construction companies who hope to benefit with fat public works contracts after their candidate is voted into office.

"The big construction companies are very generous with their contributions. However they rarely admit to having made any significant contributions for fear of being accused of corruption," Torquato said.

Brazil's federal government provides no financial assistance for politicians running for office. However most candidates win free daily airtime on television and radio under a complex system tied to the number of votes their party won in the last election.

Wary of accusations of having benefited candidates of his own Brazil Social Democrat Party (PSDB), President Fernando Henrique Cardoso warned party members against using the government machine in favor of their campaigns.
Nonetheless, the opposition accused the Cardoso administration of handing out radio licenses to a powerful evangelical group in exchange for its endorsement of the president's party's candidates.
